new_statements.translation: Note that secondary stress, in many cases, corresponds to a long vowel (phonetically speaking). It seems that syllable duration was the main factor for Tessmann in his indications of stress (marked with an acute accent). However, my preliminary data suggest that the principal correlates of primary stress are pitch (tone) and intensity.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: (pdfTeX, 19 pp., text), p.10, sec. 3 'Datos linguisticos' -- the three Spanish sentences ('Fijese en que el estres secundario.. corresponde a una vocal larga.. Parece que la duracion silabica era el factor principal para Tessmann.. Sin embargo, mis datos preliminares sugieren que los correlatos principales del estres primario son el tono y la intensidad.') are present verbatim (extracted text). Cuadro 1 on p.11 has exactly the 20 lexemes named; I re-counted the acute (primary) mark: final 14 (puRme, tSua:, o:pi, lu:ne, maRiaBe, a:ne, ejmane, japu, babane, Rawana, ma:ma, lawtome, tSa:ne, ala:maRe), penult 5 (tSa:tanI, napitSu, ta:tan@, maRatSi, natSuRi), initial 1 (tunitSa) -- m…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No positional stress rule is stated anywhere. In 2011 O'Hagan transcribes a primary stress (acute) whose correlates are pitch and intensity and a secondary stress (grave) tied to phonetic vowel length; in his 20-item table the primary stress is word-final in 14 of 20 items, penultimate in 5, initial in 1 (my count). By 2022/2023 he reanalyses this prominence as tone: most nouns end in a high tone in isolation (as in neighbouring Urarina), with a lexical H-L contrast shown by a few nouns lacking final H (pápà 'father'); the 2023 chapter (p. 951 snippet) notes Tessmann's 1920s accent marks frequently sit on different syllables from the modern high tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 2011: 'secondary stress' (grave accent) said to correspond in many cases to a phonetically long vowel, typically on the first syllable (e.g. ò:pí, lù:né, mà:má).
new_statements.exceptions: Non-final primary stress in tSà:tánI 'hombre', napítSu 'pava', tà:tánə 'paujil', maRátSi 'perro', natSúRi 'wiracocha', túnitSa 'remo' (2011 table); 2023: pápà 'father' the only disyllable with the H-L pattern (snippet).
new_statements.domain_note: All data are citation forms of c. 20-40 isolated nouns elicited from rememberers/semi-speakers (José Manuel Macusi Nuribe 2011; Juan and Jorge Macusi Nuribe 2013); 'in isolation' explicitly. No phrase-level data. Language functionally extinct; analysis necessarily preliminary.
new_statements.identity_note: Omurano proper (omur1241; a.k.a. Humurana/Roamaina/Mayna, not to be confused with Maynas), as remembered by Urarina-dominant semi-speakers of the Macusi family on the lower/middle Urituyacu in 2011-2013; c. 20-40 nouns in isolation. Glottolog's second 'phonology' ref for this languoid (Zehetner 1978, Die Mundart der Hallertau) is a Bavarian German dialect monograph mis-attached to omur1241 and irrelevant.

tone_statements.citation: O'Hagan, Zachary. 2023. Omurano. In P. Epps & L. Michael (eds.), Amazonian Languages: An International Handbook, vol. 2: Language Isolates II: Kanoé to Yurakaré, 939-956. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.
tone_statements.quote: Omurano exhibits two surface tones, high and low. Attested tonal patterns per syllable count in roots are summarized in Table 3. [Table 3: sigma-sigma LH, HL; sigma-sigma-sigma LLH, LHL, HLL; sigma-sigma-sigma-sigma LLLH, LHLH; fn. 6: HL is attested only once, in the putative loan papa 'father'.] ... First, it seems that some roots are not specified for tone. Given the absence of an attested all-low root, I consider such roots to be assigned a default final high tone. This is evident in the behavior of nouns that receive a single final high tone in isolation, and also a single final high tone when suffixed with the accusative suffix -ta (e.g., [puRima], [puRimata] 'agouti'). It follows, then, that nouns that in isolation receive a high tone on a non-final syllable must be specified for high tone (e.g., /napiCu/ -> [napiCu]). ... This suggests that a high tone may spread one syllable rightward at a morpheme boundary onto a toneless syllable, and from there all remaining syllables receive low tone. Omurano tone, however, also exhibits stress-like properties, most notably the reduction of vowels in low-toned syllables (e.g., [Rawene] 'child'). Unfortunately little more can be said of
tone_statements.locator: Section 3.4 Prosody, printed pp. 6-7; Table 3 and fn. 6 on p. 6; conclusion restated p. 13 (Section 7)
tone_statements.check: quotation from the author's open copy, read 2026-09-25; not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Confirms the catalog's 'tonal / lexical-tone' coding and supplies the rule the entry lacks: two surface tones H and L; roots are 2-4 syllables (no monosyllables, 'disyllabic minimum word requirement', p. 6); toneless roots get a default final H (no all-L root attested), roots with a non-final H are lexically specified for H; H spreads one syllable rightward across a morpheme boundary onto a tonele
